chapter_theme: Manimekalai's tears for her parents spoil Madhavi's garland, and she must fetch fresh flowers; Sudhamathi, herself once carried off from a garden by a sky-being, rules out every garden but the Buddha's Uvavanam, whose crystal pavilion and lotus seat she describes, the seat built to prove that a deed without intention bears no fruit. Walking through the festival street past a drunk pleading with a naked ascetic, a raving man in ash, a eunuch dancer and the start of Murugan's procession, the girl is surrounded by a crowd that blames her mother for her tapas, and enters the grove.

manimekalai:3:1-25.reading: As Madhavi tells Vayantamalai of the suffering of Manimekalai's father and mother, the girl, hearing it, weeps onto the flower garland she is stringing; Madhavi wipes her tears and says the garland, wet with them, has lost its purity, so she must fetch fresh flowers herself, and Sudhamathi, stringing flowers beside her, answers in grief that no man who saw tears falling from the girl's eyes could turn away from one before whom Kama himself would lay down his bow, unless he were no man.
manimekalai:3:1-25.nuance: The whole errand to the grove, and so the prince's pursuit, starts from a garland spoiled by tears for Kovalan and Kannaki: Madhavi's word தூத்தகை இழந்தது (14) makes grief a pollution of an offering. Sudhamathi's warning (23-25) is that the renunciant's grief makes her more desirable, not less. The unit was extended by one line, from 24 to 25, because line 25 (பேடியர் அன்றோ ...) ends the question begun at 23.
manimekalai:3:1-25.event: Manimekalai weeps on hearing of her parents' suffering and spoils the garland; Madhavi sends her to gather fresh flowers, and Sudhamathi objects that men will not leave such a girl alone.
manimekalai:3:1-25.unit_note: Lower boundary moved from 24 to 25: Sudhamathi's question runs from line 23 to line 25 (பேடியர் அன்றோ பெற்றியின் நின்றிடின்?).

manimekalai:3:26-41.reading: Sudhamathi tells Madhavi why she is in Puhar: she is the only daughter of Kausikan, a twice-born man of Champai, and while she gathered flowers alone and unafraid in a garden, the vidyadhara Marutavegan, coming in garlands and gold to see the great festival held for the king of the gods, seized her, rose into the sky, lay with her, made her his, and then left her here and went off to his own far city.
manimekalai:3:26-41.nuance: Her own story is the argument: a girl who picks flowers alone (ஒரு தனி, 31) at festival time can be carried off, and so Manimekalai must not go alone (43). The sky-being comes to the very festival now running, so the danger is present, not past. She tells her abandonment flatly, with no blame word for him.
manimekalai:3:26-41.event: Sudhamathi tells how the vidyadhara Marutavegan carried her off from a garden in Champai, made her his and abandoned her in Puhar.
manimekalai:3:26-41.unit_note: Upper boundary moved from 25 to 26 to follow the change in 3:1-25.

manimekalai:3:42-51.reading: Sudhamathi says Manimekalai is not one to gather flowers alone, and goes through the gardens: beyond the wall the Ilavanthikai garden is full of the king's men, and on Indra's festival day men of earth do not seek out the gardens the gods take, whose trees hang unfading garlands and no bee hums in them, so knowing people keep away from the royal park, saying a spirit with a noose in its hand guards it.
manimekalai:3:42-51.nuance: The gardens are ruled out one by one for different dangers: the king's men, the gods' claim on the festival day, and a guarding spirit. Unfading garlands and silent bees are the signs of the gods' presence. The sentence that begins at 51 ends at 52 (உய்யானத்திடை உணர்ந்தோர் செல்லார்), in the next unit; the boundary was left in place because other chapters already link to 3:52-68.

manimekalai:3:52-68.reading: Sudhamathi goes on: the knowing do not enter the Champati grove where the vulture Champati, who lost his wings to the sun's heat, once sat, nor the Kavera grove where Kaveran, father of the Kaveri maiden, sat, for both are known to hold old striking spirits; but there is the Uvavanam, where many trees flower by the command of the Bhagavan, whose unfailing vow was grace, love and the great resolve to guard all life, and in it a crystal pavilion that lets no sound out but shows the body outside, with a lotus seat of shining gem where buds laid on it open and flowers never fade and are never swarmed by bees though years pass.
manimekalai:3:52-68.nuance: The one safe grove is safe because it belongs to the Buddha (பகவன்), set against two groves of old local spirits; the epic's first Buddhist place in Puhar is introduced as a refuge from anangu. The crystal pavilion that shows the body but keeps sound in is the device the next kaathai uses to shut Manimekalai away from the prince while he can see her. Line 52 finishes the sentence of 3:42-51.

manimekalai:3:69-81.reading: Sudhamathi adds what she had forgotten: if those who have taken a vow and hold a god in mind lay flowers on the seat, the flowers reach that god's feet, but if they are laid without any thought, they stay where they are; Maya made the seat so of old, showing it with flowers, to grieve the fierce ascetics who say a deed done even without intention reaches its doer, and to be proof for those who say a deed without intention comes to nothing; and other than that grove, she says, there is no fit place for Madhavi's daughter to go.
manimekalai:3:69-81.nuance: This is the epic's first doctrinal claim, made by a device rather than an argument: the seat settles a debate by showing it. The losing side is named only as வெந் திறல் நோன்பிகள், 'vow-keepers of fierce strength' (75); I tag them Jain because the view that an unintended act still binds is theirs and because the next unit's naked, fasting ascetic is called by the same word, உண்ணா நோன்பி (90, 102), but the unit does not name the school. The winning view, that the deed lies in the intention (சிந்தை), is the Buddhist one, and the seat stands in the Buddha's grove (61).

claims.claim: a deed done even without intention reaches its doer and bears fruit
a deed done without intention bears no fruit at all

manimekalai:3:69-81.unit_note: Split from 3:69-93: Sudhamathi's speech ends at line 81 (செவ்வனம் செல்லும் செம்மை தான் இலள்), and line 82 begins the walk to the grove.

manimekalai:3:82-103.reading: Saying she too will go with Manimekalai to gather flowers, Sudhamathi sets out with her down the street of chariots, where a naked ascetic of the Jain dwelling, with a water pot in a sling and a cane staff, who has left shame and clothing, grieves even for lives he cannot see and goes unwashed under a vow of fasting, is followed by a drunk who bows to his feet and pleads that the master's soul, lodged in a filthy body, should not suffer like a prisoner in a stinking cell, that his own master said toddy brings this world, the next and endless joy, that there is no killing in coconut toddy, and that if the ascetic drinks and sees the fruit of this yoga he may then cast them off.
manimekalai:3:82-103.nuance: The drunk argues on the ascetic's own ground: the Jain rule is not to harm life, and he answers that toddy kills nothing (98), so it should be allowed; he even calls drinking a yoga (100). The ascetic's practice is described without mockery (care for unseen lives, 89), and the comedy falls on the drunk who swears and begs him. Who the drunk's தலைமகன் (97) is, a teacher or a god of drink, the unit does not say; கையுதிர்க்கொணம் (101) is a rare form I read as 'you may cast us off'.
manimekalai:3:82-103.event: Sudhamathi and Manimekalai walk through the festival street, where a drunk begs a naked Jain ascetic to drink toddy.

claims.claim: drinking coconut toddy kills nothing, so an ascetic of non-harm may drink it
toddy gives this world, the next and endless joy

manimekalai:3:82-103.unit_note: New unit 82-103, from lines 82-93 of 3:69-93 and 94-103 of 3:94-109: the first item of the crowd list (the drunk's followers) ends at line 103 (களிமகன் பின்னரும்).

manimekalai:3:104-115.reading: Others stand grieving behind a crazed man who wears oleander and erukku garlands, a rag and broken twigs for clothing, white ash smeared over his whole body, babbles senseless words to all, weeps, falls, wails, shouts, worships, rises, whirls, runs, hides in a corner, stretches out and fights his own shadow, and they watch his helpless suffering.
manimekalai:3:104-115.nuance: Ash and erukku are marks the Saiva ascetic wore, and worship (தொழூஉம், 111) is among his acts, so the figure may be a god-possessed devotee seen from outside; but the narrator calls him only மையல் உற்ற மகன் (114), and the crowd's response is pity. The heaped verbs with lengthened vowels (110-113) make the line itself reel.
manimekalai:3:104-115.event: A crazed man smeared with ash raves and whirls in the street while people watch him in pity.
manimekalai:3:104-115.unit_note: New unit from lines 104-109 of 3:94-109 and 110-115 of 3:110-125: the madman's description ends at line 115 (கண்டு நிற்குநரும்).

manimekalai:3:116-125.reading: Others watch a performer in the eunuch dance, with curled beard, braided hair, coral lips, white teeth, long eyes, white ear-rolls, a brow like the crescent, red hands, young breasts, wide hips and a painted costume, the dance that the son of the one who measured the earth danced in the street of Bana's great city.
manimekalai:3:116-125.nuance: The costume is a man's beard over a woman's body, the 'turned' figure of the பேடி. The legend (Kama, Vishnu's son, dancing in Bana's city) is the one the Silappathikaram gives among Madhavi's eleven dances, so Madhavi's art is here a street show the renunciant daughter passes by.
manimekalai:3:116-125.event: A street performer dances Kama's eunuch dance before a watching crowd.
manimekalai:3:116-125.unit_note: New unit 116-125, cut from 3:110-125 at the start of the eunuch-dance item (116).

manimekalai:3:126-145.reading: In the old city loud with strangers, others stand before the paintings that skilled painters made on the white plaster of every tall brick house, likenesses of every kind of being from the spotless gods down; and in the great festival street, women lift little boys, babbling and drooling on their five-weapon amulets, decked in gold chains, beads and loose silk, onto an elephant on a golden car, saying 'see the opening of the festival of the son of the one under the banyan', and stand watching.
manimekalai:3:126-145.nuance: The festival for Indra also holds a procession for the son of Siva (ஆல் அமர் செல்வன் மகன், 144), as the first kaathai bade every god be worshipped. The infants, unable to hold their walk or their speech, stand against the girl in robes who passes them.
manimekalai:3:126-145.event: Women set their small boys on an elephant to watch the start of Murugan's festival while others gaze at the painted houses.

manimekalai:3:146-157.reading: Like the noisy crowd that gathered round Vijaya in his eunuch's guise in Virata's city, all these people gather round Manimekalai and say that the mother who put one so lovely into hard tapas is cruel and without decency, and ask whether, if she enters the grove, the swans there could match her walk, the peacocks learn her grace or the parrots equal her speech, and say it is not fitting.
manimekalai:3:146-157.nuance: The crowd's simile casts Manimekalai as Arjuna in disguise, a figure whose true nature is hidden under an assumed form, and so, unintended by the speakers, sees the robe as a costume. Their blame of Madhavi repeats on the street what Chithirapathi sent to her as the town's talk in the last kaathai.
manimekalai:3:146-157.event: The festival crowd surrounds Manimekalai and blames her mother for putting her to tapas.

claims.claim: a mother who sets a beautiful young daughter to hard tapas is cruel and lacks decency

manimekalai:3:146-157.unit_note: Lower boundary moved from 155 to 157: the crowd's speech runs to line 157 (இசையுந அல்ல').

manimekalai:3:158-171.reading: As all who said these things grieve, the grove appears as if covered by a painted cloth that skilled hands had made, its kuravam, maravam, kurunthu, konrai, tilakam, vakulam, vetchi, narantham, nagam, punnai, pidavam, thalavam, thazhai, kudasam, bamboo, asoka, serunthi, vengai, sanbakam and ilavam spreading their flowers so that her soft feet should not be marked by the ground; bowing to the Uvavanam that Sudhamathi has shown her, Manimekalai enters it with her to gather flowers.
manimekalai:3:158-171.nuance: The list of flowers of every land is a carpet laid for her feet, so the grove receives her as the street did not. She bows (தொழுதனள், 170) before entering: the grove is a shrine, as 3:52-68 said.
manimekalai:3:158-171.event: Manimekalai bows to the Uvavanam and enters it with Sudhamathi to gather flowers.
manimekalai:3:158-171.unit_note: Upper boundary moved from 156 to 158 to follow the change in 3:146-157.

links.note: Sudhamathi warns that no man who sees the weeping Manimekalai could turn away; in the next kaathai Ettikumaran's glimpse of her faded face entering the grove sends the prince after her.
links.teaches: The warning is fulfilled by exactly the beauty it named, a face dimmed by grief rather than adorned, so the renunciant's sorrow, not her old trade, is what draws the prince into the story.

links.note: Both have a vidyadhara fly down from the sky to see Puhar's festival for Indra; in the Silappathikaram he brings his beloved as a spectator, in the Manimekalai Marutavegan seizes a brahmin girl and abandons her.
links.teaches: The heavenly visitor whom the first epic uses as an admiring eye on Puhar's festival becomes in the second a seducer who strands a girl there, so the same festival that showed Madhavi's art is now a danger to an unguarded girl.

links.note: Kural 34 makes a spotless mind the whole of virtue; the Uvavanam seat shows that a flower laid without intention goes nowhere, as proof that a deed without intention bears no fruit.
links.teaches: The couplet puts the mind first in judging virtue; the seat pushes that principle to the disputed case of the unintended act and makes it a point on which schools divided, which the couplet never has to face.

gains.a: a general ethical statement, free of any school, behind the Buddhist side of the dispute
gains.b: a hard case, the deed done without any thought, that tests how far the mind-first rule reaches

links.note: Kural 929 says reasoning with a drunk is like searching with fire under water; here the drunk reasons with a sober ascetic, arguing that toddy kills nothing.
links.teaches: The epic reverses the couplet's direction, letting the drunk be the one who argues, and his argument from non-harm shows that the drunkard's reasons can borrow the ascetic's own principle and still be worthless.

gains.a: the rule that makes the drunk's reasoning absurd without the narrator having to answer it
gains.b: a scene where the drunk himself offers reasons, showing the futility runs both ways

links.note: The drunk calls toddy-drinking a yoga whose fruit the ascetic should taste; Tirumanthiram 566 says breath-control gives the intoxication of toddy without drinking it.
links.teaches: The equation of drink and yogic ecstasy runs in opposite directions: the Tirumanthiram borrows toddy's joy as an image for breath-discipline, while the epic's drunk borrows yoga's name to sell toddy, so the pair shows the figure was common enough to be turned either way.

gains.a: evidence that 'the yoga of drink' was a live figure the epic could parody
gains.b: a satirical counter-use that shows the risk in its image of yoga as intoxication

links.note: Kundalakesi 4 calls nakedness, ash, fire and fasting mere talk and tapas a restrained life; the epic shows a naked fasting ascetic in the street, cared for unseen lives and begged to drink by a drunk.
links.teaches: The two Buddhist works keep their distance from bodily austerity by different means, argument in the fragment and street scene in the epic, and the epic allows the naked ascetic a real virtue, his pity for unseen lives, that the fragment's dismissal leaves out.

links.note: The Silappathikaram lists Kama's eunuch dance and the pot dance in Bana's city among the eleven dances Madhavi performs at Indra's festival; here a street performer dances the eunuch dance, named in nearly the same words (வாணன் பேர் ஊர் மறுகிடை ... நீள் நிலம் அளந்தோன்), as her daughter passes in robes.
links.teaches: The dance that was Madhavi's art on the royal stage at one festival is a street show at the next, watched by the crowd while her daughter walks past it to the Buddha's grove, so the repeated formula marks how far the family has moved from that stage.

links.note: In the last kaathai the town's talk, brought by Vayantamalai, calls Madhavi's tapas shameful; here the festival crowd says it to Manimekalai's face and calls the mother cruel.
links.teaches: The gossip that reached Madhavi indirectly becomes a crowd around the daughter, and its charge shifts from the mother's shame to her cruelty to the girl, so the town's judgment follows the renunciation from one generation to the next.

new_concepts.label_source: the kaathai's own words: பெரு விழா (35), விழாக் கொள் நல் நாள் (47), விழவு ஆற்றுப் படுத்த (132), விழாக் கால்கோள் (144)

source_issues: Line 100 (தெளிந்து) was repaired by the build from an old-font ௌ for ெள; the reading is secure.
Line 101 கையுதிர்க்கொணம் is a rare form; the drunk's last clause is read as 'you may cast us off', which is uncertain.

The automatic cut split speeches at lines 24/25, 155/156, and ran the crowd list across units; eight units were re-cut to sense breaks (see unit_note). The sentence of 3:42-51 ends at line 52, left in place because other chapters link to 3:52-68.
